newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FTC head cautions on defense mergers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FTC head cautions on defense mergers.

text.p: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Robert Pitofsky, whose agency will consider the merger of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas, said Thursday there must be an eventual halt to mergers in the defense industry.
"As long as there were three or four firms left, downsizing makes great sense," he said in an interview.

"When there are only two left or when there's only one left then -- both from the point of view of the Pentagon protecting its own interests and from the point of view of the anti-trust laws protecting the taxpayers interest -- you've got to call a halt somewhere," Pitofsky said.
Pitofsky's FTC has backed every defense merger that has come before it, although sometimes it has sought changes, he recalled.
"I think what's happened up until now makes great sense," he said without predicting what would happen in the future.

FTC commissioners and staff are barred by law from talking about pending cases. Two agencies have jurisdiction over anti-trust laws, the Justice Department and the FTC. Attorney General Janet Reno made it clear earlier this month that the FTC would be reviewing the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas announced their proposed merger on Dec. 15. At the time, Boeing CEO Phil Condit predicted it would take about six months to win regulatory approval.
The merged company -- to be known as Boeing -- would be the largest aerospace firm in the world. The second largest would be Lockheed-Martin Corp.
Joe Campbell, an aerospace analyst with Lehman Brothers in New York, said he thought Pitofsky was not signalling problems with the Boeing deal.
Campbell noted there was little overlap in the kinds of weapons Boeing and McDonnell Douglas produced and that Boeing was predominantly a commercial airplane firm.
"The head of the FTC has to answer that they will review these things carefully," he said in a telephone interview.
Campbell said that even with such a merger there would still be a number of suppliers available to the government, depending on which kinds of weapons one was talking about.
